title: Comets bring cyanide, a building block of life, but hitting Earth at 28 km/s cooks it
body: On 28 October 2026 Richard Anslow and colleagues at the University of Cambridge reported in [Scientific Reports](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-74214-y) that comets almost never delivered hydrogen cyanide, HCN, intact to the early Earth, though comets carry it and it helps build the molecules of life. The trouble is speed: a comet hits Earth at about 28 km/s on average, and never below 11 km/s, Earth’s own escape speed. Energy of motion per kilogram is half the speed squared, about 400 megajoules at 28 km/s, nearly a hundred times TNT, and the shock turns it into heat. In the simulations the team builds on, by [McDonald and colleagues](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.08727), HCN breaks apart above about 3,600 kelvin within a fraction of a second: for a 1 km comet hitting head-on, about 98% survives at 5 km/s, 38% at 8, 2% at 10 and none above 15, while a grazing hit heats far less. The air also breaks up comets under about 100 m, and an ocean dilutes whatever lands. Of over 100,000 comets above 100 m that struck the early Earth, the best case gives 87 useful deliveries and 54% of simulated histories give none; Mars, hit at about 20 km/s through thin air, gets 744.

slides.question: A comet hits Earth at 28 km/s. Its energy of motion per kilogram is how many times that of a kilogram of TNT?
slides.explanation: About 95: half the speed squared gives roughly 400 megajoules per kilogram, against 4.2 for TNT. The impact shock turns that energy into heat of thousands of degrees.

slides.alt: Animation on black space: a cyan comet and the molecule H–C≡N, a comet falling onto Earth at 28.2 km/s, a comet glowing red beside a temperature bar marking 3,600 and 7,000 K, a survival curve falling to zero by 15 km/s, head-on and grazing hits, 100 tiles with 54 red, bars Earth 87, Mars 744.

slides.prompt: Keep the comet’s cyanide alive at Earth’s average impact speed of 28 km/s. What angle does it take?
slides.takeaway: Only a graze: at 28 km/s head-on the shock reaches about 25,000 K, far past the 3,600 K where HCN breaks; below about 17° it stays under. In the models, heat scales with sin(angle)^1.6.

slides.heading: Hydrogen cyanide surviving a head-on hit by a 1 km comet
slides.note: Simulations by McDonald and colleagues (2025) that the new study builds on; equilibrium chemistry.

left.label: Earth: 87
left.text: Comets arrive at about 28 km/s on average through thick air, and most land in the ocean. In 54% of simulated histories, not one delivery succeeds.

right.label: Mars: 744
right.text: A smaller planet with thin air is hit at about 20 km/s on average, so more comets stay slow and cool enough for the cyanide to survive.

slides.question: Why does a comet hitting Earth at 28 km/s destroy most of the hydrogen cyanide it carries?
options: The impact shock heats it past 3,600 K
Sunlight breaks it on the way in
slides.explanation: Energy per kilogram grows with the square of the speed, and the shock turns it into heat. Above about 3,600 kelvin HCN falls apart in a fraction of a second; only slow, grazing hits stay cool enough.
